title: What STAR stands for
question: An interviewer says: "Please answer using the STAR method." What does the acronym describe?
options: Skills, Training, Achievements, References: a way to present your CV in order of importance
Strategy, Team, Approach, Review: a checklist for planning a new software project
Situation, Task, Action, Result: a structure for telling a concrete story about past work
Summary, Technology, Architecture, Roadmap: a template for describing a system design
explanation: STAR organises a behavioral answer into the Situation (context), the Task (your responsibility), the Action (what you did) and the Result (what happened). It keeps the story concrete and easy to follow. The other expansions sound professional but are not what interviewers mean by the term.

title: Where the STAR answer spends its time
question: When telling a STAR story, which part should usually take the largest share of your answer?
options: The Action, because it shows your own decisions and the steps you took
The Situation, because the interviewer needs every detail of the background to judge you
The Task, because a long description of the assignment proves you understood the goal
The Result, because the final numbers matter more than how the work was done
explanation: Interviewers use behavioral questions to learn how you work, and that is visible in the Action: what you decided, tried and communicated. Situation and Task should be brief setup, and the Result closes the story with the outcome. Long context or an outcome without a method leaves the main question unanswered.

title: 'I' versus 'we' in a team story
question: You are asked about a group project from your bootcamp. The interviewer says: "What was your part in it?" Which way of answering works best?
options: Keep saying "we" throughout, so the interviewer sees that you value teamwork above individual credit in every answer
Summarise what the team delivered overall, since the final product is what the interviewer cares about
Claim the whole project as your own, so that the interviewer clearly sees your leadership potential
Describe the specific pieces you built or decided, using "I", and still credit the team where it helped
explanation: The interviewer is hiring you, not the team, so they need to hear your contribution. Using "I" for your own work and "we" for shared outcomes is honest and shows you can collaborate. Hiding behind "we" hides your role, summaries avoid the question, and claiming other people's work is dishonest and easy to expose with follow-ups.

title: Closing a STAR story with a result
question: You are finishing a story about speeding up a slow page in your portfolio app. Which closing sentence is the strongest Result?
options: "After my changes the page felt much faster, and everybody on the team was very happy with it and with the result"
"Load time went from about 4 seconds to under 1.5, and I documented the fix so the team reused it"
"I learned a lot about performance tooling and I am excited to keep improving as an engineer"
"The page was eventually fixed, and the project moved on to the next set of tasks on the roadmap"
explanation: A good Result is specific: a measurable change (even from a personal project) and its consequence. Vague satisfaction ("felt faster", "everybody was happy") cannot be checked, a lesson alone does not say what changed, and "eventually fixed" does not credit your action. Numbers you can explain make the story credible.

title: How long a STAR answer should be
question: In a 45-minute interview you plan to give six behavioral answers. Roughly how long should a single STAR answer last so you can cover the ground and still let the interviewer follow up?
options: Under thirty seconds, so that the interviewer can cover as many topics as possible in the conversation
Five minutes or more, so that every step of the story is told in chronological detail
As long as it takes to mention every project on your CV that relates to the question
Around two minutes, which leaves room for the interviewer to ask follow-up questions
explanation: About one and a half to two minutes is enough to cover all four parts and still let the interviewer dig deeper. Thirty seconds is usually too thin to be convincing, long chronological stories lose the listener, and listing several projects makes each one shallow. Practising aloud helps you find the right length.

title: Choosing a story with no work experience
question: In a first interview you hear: "Tell me about a time you solved a hard problem." You have never had a job as a developer. What is the best choice?
options: Explain that you have no professional experience yet and offer to answer a technical question instead
Pick a real challenge from your capstone, course or personal project and tell it in STAR form, focusing on your own steps
Describe a work-style story from a past non-tech job, even if it has nothing to do with the problem asked and hope the interviewer values it anyway
Adapt a story you heard from a developer friend as if it had happened to you, since it sounds more professional
explanation: Interviewers hiring juniors expect examples from education and projects; what matters is a real problem, your reasoning and a result. Deflecting wastes the chance to show how you think. A non-tech story can work when it is relevant, but ignoring the question does not, and presenting someone else's story as yours is a lie that follow-up questions quickly reveal.

title: Fixing a story that is all background
question: After a practice interview, your mentor says that your answers spend two minutes on the team, the tech stack and the client before reaching what you did. What should you change?
options: Compress Situation and Task into two or three sentences and move quickly to the specific actions you took
Drop the Situation entirely and start every answer with the Action, since context is what bores interviewers
Keep the same background but speak faster so the whole story still fits inside the available time
Replace the story with a list of your technical skills, which is shorter and easier for interviewers to scan
explanation: The setup only needs enough context to make the Action understandable: where, what was at stake and what you were responsible for. Removing it completely makes the story confusing, speeding up keeps the imbalance and hurts clarity, and a list of skills does not answer a behavioral question, which asks for evidence of behavior.

title: A STAR story whose project was cancelled
question: Your best example is a team project that was cancelled before launch, so there are no user numbers. How should you handle the Result part?
options: Make up an adoption figure, because a story without numbers is rarely taken seriously by hiring teams that screen many juniors a day
Skip the Result and end on the Action, since the outcome was out of your control and may distract from it
State the real outcome, then share what you delivered, what you measured or learned, and what you changed afterwards
Choose a different story at random, because a cancelled project can never demonstrate anything useful
explanation: A Result does not have to be a launch metric. Honest outcomes such as tests added, deadlines met, a demo accepted or a lesson that changed your later work still show impact and self-awareness. Inventing numbers risks your credibility, omitting the Result leaves the story unfinished, and abandoning a good example throws away real evidence.

title: Answering 'tell me about yourself'
question: The first question of the interview is: "Tell me about yourself." Which structure makes the best answer for a junior developer?
options: A chronological story of your life starting in school, including every course and hobby along the way and each early job you had
A short pitch: what you do now, the projects or studies that prepared you, and why this role fits what you want next
A line-by-line reading of your CV, so the interviewer hears every item that is already printed on it
A brief reply that you are hardworking and a fast learner, leaving the interviewer to ask for details
explanation: This question invites a focused present, past and future summary tied to the job. A full life story is unfocused, reading the CV aloud adds nothing new, and generic adjectives give the interviewer nothing concrete to explore. Keep it to about a minute and end by connecting to the role.

title: Answering 'why this company?'
question: The interviewer asks: "Why do you want to work here?" Which answer is most convincing?
options: Say that the company is a well-known name and that it would look great on your CV for future jobs and open doors at other companies
Explain that you are applying to many companies and this one simply happened to answer first
Say that you would be happy anywhere that offers a chance, because as a junior you cannot be picky
Mention something specific you learned about the product, team or engineering culture and link it to your own goals
explanation: A specific, researched reason shows real interest and lets the interviewer see how you would fit. Prestige alone, a numbers game or "anywhere will do" may all be true in part, but they say nothing about this company and suggest you might leave at the first alternative.

title: Why do you want to be a developer?
question: A hiring manager asks why you chose software development, especially if you changed careers. What is the best way to answer?
options: Share the real moment or project that sparked your interest and show how you have kept building since then
Say that the field pays well and has many openings, since that is a practical and honest reason for someone starting out
Say that you have always loved computers and always knew this would be your career, without examples
Say that your previous career was not working out, and that development was the next logical option
explanation: A genuine story with evidence of continued effort (courses, projects, practice) is memorable and hard to fake. Pay and job availability may be true but make the choice sound purely transactional, a claim of lifelong passion without examples sounds rehearsed, and dwelling on what went wrong before gives a negative frame instead of what draws you here.

title: Questions to ask at the end
question: At the end of the interview you hear: "Do you have any questions for us?" What is the best response?
options: Say that everything was already covered, to show respect for the interviewer's time at the end of the day and avoid repeating topics
Ask right away about vacation days, remote policy and the exact date of the first salary review
Ask thoughtful questions about onboarding, code review, mentoring and what success looks like in the first months
Ask what the company does, since you did not have enough time to research it before the interview
explanation: Good questions show curiosity and help you judge the team, especially how juniors are supported. Declining to ask can look uninterested, asking only about perks first can seem to put benefits before the work, and asking basic questions the website answers shows lack of preparation. Benefits are fine to discuss at the right stage.

title: Talking about a weakness
question: You are asked: "What is your biggest weakness?" Which answer works best for a junior developer?
options: Say that you are a perfectionist who works too hard, since that turns the weakness into a strength and shows how committed you are
Say that you honestly do not have significant weaknesses and prefer to let the interviewer judge
Name a real, work-relevant weakness, such as hesitating to ask for help, and explain what you are doing about it
Name a serious weakness like missing deadlines and explain that you are still figuring it out
explanation: The interviewer wants self-awareness and evidence of growth. A disguised strength sounds evasive, claiming no weaknesses sounds unaware, and a core problem with no plan for improvement raises concerns. A real, manageable weakness plus concrete steps (for example, setting a time limit before asking for help) is credible.

title: Disagreeing with a teammate
question: The interviewer asks: "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate." Which story and framing is best?
options: A technical disagreement where you listened, compared options with evidence and agreed on a path, even when it was not yours
A disagreement where you convinced the team to adopt your idea, which shows that you can lead others by presenting a clear, well-prepared case
A story in which you avoided conflict entirely and quietly did what the teammate wanted to keep peace
A case where the teammate was clearly wrong, and you explain in detail how you proved their mistake
explanation: Interviewers look for respectful communication, openness to other views and focus on the problem, not winning. Showing that you can commit to a decision you did not make is a strong signal. Winning stories can sound inflexible, silent avoidance hides your voice, and proving someone wrong makes the story about blame instead of collaboration.

title: Handling an impossible deadline
question: You are asked how you handle tight deadlines. Which example shows the most mature approach?
options: Working nights and weekends until everything planned was delivered, showing commitment to the team's goals every time
Delivering the full scope on time by skipping tests and cleaning up the shortcuts after the release
Waiting until the last days to see whether the deadline could still be met before mentioning any risk
Estimating early, telling the team what would slip, agreeing on a smaller scope and delivering that on time
explanation: Handling pressure well means prioritising, communicating risk early and negotiating scope, not just working harder. Overwork is not sustainable and hides planning problems, skipping tests transfers cost to later, and staying quiet about risk removes the team's chance to adjust.

title: Teamwork when you only have projects
question: The interviewer says: "All your experience is personal and course projects. How can I know you will work well in a team?" What is the best answer?
options: Explain that solo projects require more skills than team projects, so teamwork will come naturally to you without any extra practice
Point to concrete collaboration: pull requests, code reviews, issues, pair programming or open source, with what you learned
Promise to be a quick learner and a great team player, and offer a trial period without any pay
Say that you are comfortable working alone and will need little help from teammates in the first months
explanation: The concern is real, so address it with evidence: collaboration artifacts such as reviewed pull requests, group work and open-source contributions. Dismissing the concern, relying on promises or offering free work, and stressing independence all fail to show how you behave with others, which is what the interviewer wants to see.

title: Answering 'tell me about a mistake'
question: You are asked about a time you made a mistake. Which answer is the most effective?
options: A tiny, harmless slip such as a typo, so that the interviewer sees how rarely you make errors
A mistake caused mostly by unclear instructions, explaining why the situation was not really your fault and the team's process
A claim that you cannot recall any significant mistakes, since you always double-check your work
A real mistake of moderate size, owned plainly, with what you did to fix it and what you do differently now
explanation: Interviewers want honesty, accountability and learning. A mistake that is real but not catastrophic, told without excuses and ending in a changed habit, shows maturity. Trivial slips, shifting blame and claiming no mistakes all avoid the question and make the answer less believable.

title: A technical question you cannot answer
question: In a technical interview you are asked how a message queue guarantees delivery, and you have never used one. What is the best response?
options: Give a confident answer built from guesses, because showing hesitation costs more than being slightly wrong in the eyes of a hiring panel
Say you have not used one, then explain what you do know, reason aloud about how it might work and say how you would learn it
Say that you do not know and ask to move on to the next question, to avoid wasting the interviewer's time
Say it is not relevant to junior work and steer the conversation to a topic where you are stronger
explanation: Honesty plus visible reasoning lets the interviewer assess how you think, which matters more than a single fact for a junior. Bluffing is usually detected and damages trust, giving up immediately shows no curiosity, and dismissing the question sounds defensive. Relating it to something you know, such as retries or acknowledgements, shows transferable understanding.

title: Vague problem in a live coding round
question: In a live coding round you receive a one-sentence problem: "Design a function that finds duplicate users." You are unsure what counts as a duplicate. What should you do first?
options: Start coding the simplest interpretation right away, since silence while thinking can look like being stuck in front of the interviewer
Pick the most advanced interpretation you can imagine to show that you are comfortable with hard problems
Ask clarifying questions about what makes users equal and the data size, then state your assumptions before coding
Wait quietly and think about the problem until the answer is clear, so you do not interrupt with questions
explanation: Clarifying requirements is part of real engineering work, and interviewers often leave problems ambiguous on purpose. Asking and stating assumptions shows communication and care. Jumping into code risks solving the wrong problem, over-engineering ignores the actual need, and long silence gives the interviewer no view of your reasoning.

title: Explaining a gap on your CV
question: Your CV shows an eight-month gap before you started learning to code. The interviewer asks about it. Which answer is best?
options: Briefly state the reason in a neutral way, then focus on what you learned and built since and why you are ready now
Give a long, detailed account of the personal difficulties behind the gap, so the interviewer fully understands your situation
Say that you were taking a break and had no particular plans, to avoid claiming activities that did not happen
Say that you were working on freelance projects, even though that was not exactly the case, to fill the time
explanation: A short, honest explanation followed by a forward-looking story keeps control of the narrative. You do not owe private details, and over-sharing can make the answer heavy. Offering nothing leaves a negative impression, while inventing activities is a lie that can end an offer if discovered during reference checks.

title: Interviewer spots a bug in your code
question: While you code live, the interviewer says: "I think this loop skips the last element." You had not noticed. What is the best reaction?
options: Defend the code first and explain why it should work, since conceding too fast can look like a lack of confidence
Thank them, trace an example by hand to confirm, explain the cause aloud and fix it, then re-check the edge cases
Apologise several times and say that you are nervous, so the interviewer understands why the mistake happened
Quickly change the loop bound without comment, hoping the fix goes unnoticed and the flow of the session continues
explanation: Interviewers often point out bugs to see how you take feedback. Verifying the claim, fixing it calmly and thinking aloud shows humility and method. Defending without checking shows rigidity, repeated apologies draw attention to nerves instead of the solution, and a silent change hides the reasoning they want to observe.

title: 'Why do you think you are ready?'
question: You feel like an impostor and the interviewer asks: "Why do you think you are ready for a professional role?" What is the best answer?
options: Say that you are fully ready for anything and show certainty to hide any doubts about your level from everyone on the hiring panel
Say that you are not sure and that the interviewer should decide whether to give you a chance
Say that many people with the same background got hired, so you should reasonably qualify as well
Be honest that you are early in your career and point to evidence: what you built, how you learn and what you contributed
explanation: Feeling like an impostor is common, and the answer is grounded evidence rather than either overconfidence or self-doubt. Claiming you are ready for anything is not believable for a junior, handing the decision to the interviewer sounds passive, and comparing yourself to others says nothing about your own readiness.

title: Realising your approach is wrong mid-interview
question: Twenty minutes into a 45-minute coding interview, you realise your solution cannot handle a case the interviewer just mentioned. What is the best move?
options: Say it clearly, explain why it fails, outline a better approach and ask whether to rewrite or keep the working part
Patch the code with special cases until the new example passes, keeping the original design so no time is lost in the interview
Keep going quietly with the current approach and hope the interviewer does not test the failing case again
Restart from scratch in silence with a new idea, since explaining the failure would only waste remaining time
explanation: Recognising a flawed design and recovering is exactly what happens on real projects, and interviewers value explicit reasoning and collaboration more than a perfect first attempt. Piling special cases creates fragile code, hoping the case is forgotten is a gamble that hides the problem, and silent restarts give the interviewer nothing to evaluate.

title: A skill you listed but barely used
question: Your CV lists Kubernetes because you followed one tutorial. The interviewer, impressed, starts asking about production cluster upgrades. What is the best response?
options: Answer with general knowledge and confident wording, then steer toward the topics you know better and avoid admitting how limited your experience is
Explain that the CV is a summary and that you have worked with the tool enough to discuss it in depth
Clarify that your experience is limited to a tutorial, describe exactly what you did and learned, and say how you would deepen it
Say that the experience was long ago and you have forgotten the details, hoping to end the line of questions
explanation: Overstating skills is a common junior trap; correcting the impression yourself protects your credibility and shows integrity, while the hands-on details show you did learn something. Bluffing or inflating the experience is likely to be exposed with follow-up questions, and claiming forgetfulness is evasive. Fix the CV wording afterwards so it states the real level.

title: Purpose of the recruiter screen
question: A recruiter invites you to a 20-minute call before any technical interview. What is the main purpose of this call?
options: To check basic fit and logistics such as interest, availability, expectations and process, and to answer your questions
To assess your coding ability in depth, so that weaker candidates are removed before the interviews with engineers even begin
To make the final hiring decision, since recruiters usually have the last word on junior candidates
To negotiate the final offer, because the details of the package are normally closed in the first call
explanation: The recruiter screen is a short filter on motivation, background, availability, expectations and the next steps, and it is your chance to ask about the process and the role. Deep technical assessment and final decisions come later from the engineering team, and the real negotiation happens when there is an offer.

title: Salary expectation in the first call
question: In the recruiter screen you hear: "What are your salary expectations?" You have no benchmark yet. What is the best way to respond?
options: Say that money is not important to you at this stage and that you will accept whatever is offered so that the company sees how motivated you are
Name the highest figure you have heard of for a junior, expecting the company to bargain downward
Research typical ranges for the role and location, share a reasonable range and say that you are open to the whole package
Refuse to discuss it at all and say that you will only talk numbers once the company makes an offer
explanation: Answering with a researched range anchors the conversation in facts and signals flexibility. Saying you will accept anything gives away leverage, an inflated figure may end the process early, and a flat refusal can seem uncooperative. If you are unsure, you can ask about the budgeted range for the role. Ranges differ by market, so research your own.

title: Comparing two first offers
question: Company A offers a slightly higher base salary but a solo-developer role with no code review. Company B offers a bit less, with senior mentors and structured onboarding. How should you decide?
options: Take the higher base salary, because early-career income compounds and learning can happen on your own time
Weigh the whole picture, including learning, mentoring and growth, against your financial needs, rather than base salary alone
Take whichever offer arrived first, since delaying the decision can only reduce your chances with both companies and make you look indecisive
Take the company with the more recognisable name, because that brand carries more weight on future CVs
explanation: For a first job, the quality of mentoring, feedback and growth can shape the next years of your career, but you also need to cover your costs, so weigh both. Base salary is only one part of the package, speed is not a decision criterion, and brand alone says little about what you will actually learn there.

title: Asking for time to decide
question: You receive a written offer by email but you still have a final interview elsewhere next week. What is the best way to respond?
options: Accept immediately to secure the job, and withdraw later if the other process turns out better for you once you know more about both
Stay silent for a few days to see what happens elsewhere, then reply once you know where you stand
Say that you have a better offer pending, so that they raise the numbers before the deadline arrives
Thank them, show enthusiasm, ask for a reasonable deadline, and be open about the reason without naming other companies
explanation: A polite request for a few days is normal, and a courteous, honest tone keeps goodwill. Accepting while planning to withdraw harms your reputation and the company, silence reads as disinterest and may let the offer lapse, and bluffing about a better offer is dishonest and can backfire if they simply move on.

title: Negotiating politely as a junior
question: An offer arrives slightly below the range you researched. You like the team and want to ask for more. What is the best approach?
options: Accept as it is, because a junior has little leverage and negotiating risks the offer being withdrawn, and you can always ask again after a year of good work
Say that you have bills to pay and need more money, because honesty about your needs is persuasive
Express enthusiasm, ask if there is flexibility, support the request with market research and mention non-salary items like learning budget
Send a firm counteroffer demanding the figure and say that you will walk away if it is not matched
explanation: Most employers expect a polite, reasoned conversation, and tying the request to research and to the whole package (training, review dates, equipment) keeps it collaborative. Not asking forfeits a legitimate chance, personal needs are not a business argument, and ultimatums harm the relationship before you have even started.

title: Declining an offer professionally
question: You decided to accept another offer and must decline the one from a company whose team you liked. What is the best way to do it?
options: Reply promptly with thanks, give a brief honest reason and say that you would be glad to stay in touch
Stop replying to the recruiter's emails, since a refusal that is never said cannot cause any awkwardness
Explain in detail everything you disliked about their process, so the company can improve in the future
Wait until the offer deadline has passed so that you keep the option open as long as possible
explanation: A prompt, courteous decline protects relationships, and the tech community is small. Ghosting is unprofessional and wastes their time, long criticism is unsolicited and can come across as harsh, and waiting past the deadline only delays the company's next candidate. A brief reason is enough; you do not owe a full explanation.

title: An offer expiring before your top choice responds
question: Company A's offer expires in two days. Your preferred Company B is still a week from its final round. You want to keep both options. What is the best approach?
options: Tell B that you already hold a competing offer at a higher salary, so that they decide faster and the final round can be brought forward
Accept A to be safe and tell B nothing, then decide later whether to withdraw if B makes an offer
Let A's offer expire and wait for B, because accepting under time pressure usually leads to regret
Ask A politely for a short extension, tell B about the deadline and ask if the process can speed up, and be accurate throughout
explanation: Honest communication is the best lever: companies commonly extend a deadline or speed up when they know a candidate has another process. Exaggerating the other offer is a lie that can sour both relationships, accepting and then backing out harms your reputation, and letting a real offer lapse removes your safety net without any guarantee from B.

title: Employee contract versus contractor-style offer
question: One company offers a regular employment contract, another a contractor-style arrangement with a higher monthly figure. Their legal rules vary by country. What is the best way to compare them?
options: Choose the higher monthly figure, since the extra amount clearly compensates for whatever is missing in the contract
Compare the total package: benefits, stability, notice terms, taxes and your own obligations, and read the contract carefully
Choose the employment contract, because it is always the better option for a junior regardless of the numbers or the type of work
Choose whichever the recruiter recommends, since the company knows its own contract types better than you
explanation: The headline number hides differences such as paid leave, insurance, retirement contributions, notice periods, who pays taxes and how stable the work is. Compare net amounts and protections, read the terms, and ask someone who knows your local rules if needed. Always preferring one type, or trusting the recruiter's view alone, ignores your own situation.
